Items.Authors: Paolo Dal Bo, Mario De Lucia, Andrea Limonta, Andrea Tartari, Giovanni Signorelli, Tommaso Lari, Mario Zannoni, Michele Pinchera, Eugenia Di Giorgi, Andrea Passerini, Maurizio Massa, Keteryna Leonova, Luca Porcelli, Giovanni Delle Monache, Massimo Rossella, Domenico Calabro, Andrea Moggi, Fabio Tramonti, Lorenzo Zanga, Gabriele Coppi, Alessandro Novelli, Graeme Smecher, Joshua Montgomery, Matt Dobbs, Jean-François Cliche, Donato Nicolò
Items.Title: Progress on the path towards the TRL6 qualification of the LiteBIRD SQUID Controller Unit
Items.Abstract: LiteBIRD is a JAXA-led satellite mission planned for the 2030s to measure CMB polarization and search for the faint B-mode signal of inflation. Detecting this signal requires ultra-low-noise, polarization-sensitive TES bolometers read out with digital frequency-division multiplexing using LC filters and SQUID amplifiers. The warm electronics include the Signal-Processing Assembly, Digitizer Assembly, and the SQUID Controller Assembly (SCA), which provides SQUID biasing and preamplification for four channels. INFN is responsible for designing and space-qualifying the SQUID Controller Unit (SCU), which integrates eight SCAs in a dedicated enclosure with mechanical support, thermal interface, and EMI shielding. This work reports the SCU qualification toward TRL6, including functional tests on a single SCA and environmental tests on an SCU setup with one active SCA and seven dummies, covering thermal-vacuum, vibration, EMI, and EMC.

Items.Authors: Raveena Khan, M. S. Savitha, K. Nagaraju
Items.Title: Prototype development of a visible-light polarimeter: a path to EUV spectropolarimetry
Items.Abstract: Scientists are working to unlock the Sun’s magnetic secrets by studying how light is polarized in different wavelengths. Earlier experiments with the SOHO satellite showed the technique of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) polarization measurement could reveal magnetic fields in the Sun’s corona, but progress has been limited by the lack of sensitive polarimetric instruments. To address this, we have designed and built a polarimeter prototype using three mirrors arranged in a special design. Tested with aluminum mirrors at visible light, the reflection-based polarimeter shows verified results. Future versions will operate in the EUV range, paving the way for direct measurements of coronal magnetic fields.

Items.Authors: Thibaut Prod'Homme, Carlos Corral Van Damme, Timo Rühl, Kate Isaak, Marco Sirianni, Jens Loehring, Massimo Lucia, Massimo Falcolini, Jean-Philippe Halain, Luc Boucher, Peter Verhoeve, Eloy Hernandez, Laurence Soulat, Marc Broussely, Matthew Vaughan, Albertus Kusumo Adi, Diego Escorial Olmos, Rafael Guzmán, Santiago Serrano, Stefan Kögl, Florian Kehl, Antonio Rodríguez-Senín, Paola Kögl, Eider Ocerin, David Mateo, Juan Oñate, Eduardo Ugalde, Marcos Ubierna, Aitor Barrena, Laura Burgos, Marco Truglio, Iñigo Ojanguren, Ignacio Torralbo, Leire Benito, Yasin Tahiri, Dan Tye, Hans-Peter Gröbelbauer, Florian Wirz, Gerhard Székely, Eloi Vázquez Codesido, Clément Charuel, Etienne Lallemand, Jean-Yves Plesseria, Gabriel Giono, Harald Ottacher
Items.Title: Prototyping Arrakihs: accelerating & derisking instrument development for an ESA Fast-Class Mission
Items.Abstract: Fast-class missions in ESA’s science programme have as their main objective to nearly halve their development time compared to medium or large-class missions; 8 years from selection to launch instead of 15. In the context of this accelerated scheme, the development of bespoke high-performing instruments for space missions with attractive scientific objectives is a considerable challenge.   Using the Arrakihs mission as an example we show how prototyping during the study phase helps accelerate and derisk the development of such instruments. In this contribution, we will go through the results from more than 10 different prototyping activities from optics to detectors, from electronic boards to mechanical parts which took place during phase B and extract lessons learned.

Items.Authors: Prakamya Agrawal, SO Collaboration
Items.Title: Quantifying spurious signals from the Moon in the Small Aperture Telescope
Items.Abstract: The Simons Observatory (SO), located on Cerro Toco in the Atacama Desert in Chile, is a mm-wavelength observatory measuring intensity and polarization anisotropies at angular scales ranging from one arcminute to tens of degrees. The larger scales are the focus of the Small Aperture Telescopes (SATs). We present the findings of a study using observations of the moon with a single SAT observing in the spectral bands centered at 90 and 150 GHz. We investigate signals seen on detectors that are intentionally uncoupled to the telescope optics, searching for spurious optical coupling and electrical crosstalk.

Items.Authors: Matteo Faccioni, Patrick S. Vrancken
Items.Title: Quantifying the errors in modeling optical propagation in a turbulent atmosphere using different phase screen synthesization methods
Items.Abstract: In this publication, three different methods for synthesizing phase screens are investigated: the classical random phase method, its optimized version using the sub-harmonics method, and a new proposed method based on the phase correlation function, called correlation based method. The three methods' results are compared in terms of the aberration content, expressed using the Zernike polynomials. It is shown that the here proposed correlation based method can eliminate to a high degree the discretization errors that arise while using the discrete Fourier transform. It thus offers better accuracy w.r.t. the theoretical index of refraction fluctuations structure function, and high flexibility as it allows for generating phase screens at any desired spatial resolution on arbitrary grids (e.g., cuboids or rectangular grids) without the need of any weighting parameters.

Items.Authors: Brodi Elwood
Items.Title: Quantifying the systematic impact of differential beam response on the BICEP CMB polarization data from 2016 through 2024
Items.Abstract: As CMB polarization experiments—such as BICEP3, BICEP Array (BA), and future BICEP experiments—achieve ever-deeper polarization maps in search of primordial B-modes from inflation, constraining instrumental systematics below statistical uncertainties becomes increasingly challenging. Since the BICEP telescopes are pair-differencing experiments, differential beam response leads to T-to-P leakage, introducing potential systematic bias on the inferred tensor-to-scalar ratio r.  The lowest-order beam-mismatch modes are mitigated through deprojection, though residual undeprojected modes remain. To quantify these residuals, we perform comprehensive in-situ far-field beam measurements of the BICEP receivers. Using beam measurements from BICEP3 (95 GHz) taken in 2016-2019 and 2023; BA1-30/40 in 2020, 2023, and 2024; and BA2-150 in 2023 and 2024, we present analyses of differential beam response and assess the impact of undeprojected residuals on estimates of r for the BK24 data release.

Items.Authors: Valente Vázquez-Velázquez, Joel Sanchez-Bermudez, Carolina Keiman Freire, Fernando Angeles Uribe, Salvador Cuevas Cardona, Alejandro Farah Simon, Rubén Flores-Meza, Rebeca García-Lopez, Gerhard Ulbricht
Items.Title: Quantitative characterization and failure diagnosis in cryogenic vacuum systems using distributed pressure and temperature instrumentation
Items.Abstract: The optimal performance of astronomical detectors depends critically on thermal stability and vacuum integrity during qualification tests. Failures in cooling or vacuum loss risk sensitive optomechanical payloads. This work presents a metrological characterization system developed at the Institute of Astronomy of the UNAM designed for real-time thermodynamic monitoring of a cryogenic testbed. This infrastructure is crucial for testing diverse equipment destined for projects such as GRAVITY+. The setup integrates temperature and pressure sensors managed by an IoT-based data acquisition architecture. It records cooling curves and evacuation rates to correlate vacuum pressure with thermal transfer efficiency quantitatively. Results identifying anomalies like micro-leaks and outgassing are reported. This diagnostic tool validates the test environment stability, ensuring the integrity of components for satellites or telescopes during their thermal-vacuum qualification phases.

Items.Authors: Stephen T. Ridgway, Brittany M. McClinton
Items.Title: Quantum closure phase for robust imaging at the single-photon level
Items.Abstract: Closure phase enables imaging with interferometric arrays. Classically it is obtained by summing fringe phases on three baselines, each derived from a resolved fringe and stabilized optical path, which sets a hard photon-flux limit. We outline two quantum schemes that push closure measurements toward the single-photon regime.   In the Bell-pair approach, each telescope pair shares entanglement; a detected photon gives a binary outcome whose statistics depend on the phase difference. Three such events, one per baseline within the piston-stability time, form a closure sample in which telescope terms cancel without fringe formation. A second scheme, using a three-qubit GHZ state, provides a single shared phase so that one multi-site measurement yields the sum of the three local phases, sensitive to the source but including a global offset that must be calibrated. These methods could extend closure phase to targets too faint for classical interferometry.

Items.Authors: James M. Ivory, Martin Prest, Nyasha J. Suliali, Konstantin D. Stefanov, Manish R. Patel
Items.Title: Radiation damage in CIS120 for use in future space missions
Items.Abstract: This work focusses on the characterisation of the Teledyne E2v CIS120, a CMOS device planned for use in many upcoming space telescopes, with some of these interested in UV measurements.     As the main wavelengths of interest are in the UV spectrum, characterisation is primarily done on light between 200 – 400 nm, both before and after separate gamma and proton irradiations. A broad range of metrics are characterised, including dark current, noise and quantum efficiency, at room temperature, 20 °C and -25 °C.

Items.Authors: Faustine Cantalloube, Olivier Absil, Marc Van Droogenbroeck, Anthony Cioppa, Carles Cantero-Mitjans, Sébastien Piérard, Nitya Pandey
Items.Title: Ranking detection capabilities of post-processing techniques for high-contrast imaging: revisiting the Exoplanet Imaging Data Challenge phase 1
Items.Abstract: The Exoplanet Imaging Data Challenge (EIDC) is a platform that enables the high-contrast imaging (HCI) community to compare post-processing methods for different tasks, organized into different phases. In 2020 we published the results of phase 1, focused on the detection of planetary signals in data sets coming from various instruments. At the time, we used various scores to evaluate the detection performance of algorithms and provided several rankings to compare the capabilities of the 28 algorithms proposed by the 15 participants. Recently, under the impulse of the AI-based image processing community, new evaluation frameworks have emerged for ranking algorithms. Among them, the Tile is a 2-dimensional figure that displays different ranking scores for crisp two-class classifiers at a glance. In this contribution, we apply different flavors of the Tile to the results of Phase 1 of the Exoplanet Imaging Data Challenge, indicating how to analyze the performance and compare algorithms.

Items.Authors: Samantha A. Grubb
Items.Title: Ray tracing, optical modeling, and calibration of the Simons Observatory Large Aperture Telescope instrumental polarization angle
Items.Abstract: Simons Observatory (SO) is a new millimeter-wave Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) experiment located in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile. SO is designed to make precise measurements of the temperature and polarization of the CMB. It has one 6 meter Large Aperture Telescope (LAT). Its receiver includes a focal plane made up of 60,000 transition-edge sensor (TES) bolometers that are sensitive to orthogonal linear polarization states. A potential scientific goal of SO is to probe for cosmic birefringence, a rotation of the CMB polarization plane that would signal new, parity-violating physics. Small miscalibrations in detector orientation and distortions from the telescope’s optics can rotate the measured CMB polarization by an instrumental angle, α, mimicking the birefringence signal. This work focuses on determining the LAT’s instrumental polarization angle using an optical model that traces rays through the telescope’s optics to determine the on-sky polarization direction.

Items.Authors: Camilo Weinberger, Elena Masciadri, Luca Carbonaro, Fernando Pedichini, Ciro Del Vecchio, Christian Veillet, Sam Ragland, Marlene de sepibus
Items.Title: R&D activity in INAF on light instrumentation for continuous optical turbulence monitoring
Items.Abstract: Optical turbulence (OT) measurements are useful for turbulence characterization but also for the application of hybrid technics (atmospheric models plus observations) for the OT forecasts. With this in mind we started a R&D activity in INAF-Arcetri in collaboration with INAF-Rome and LBT focused on instrumentation for OT estimates. The roadmap at long time scale aims to cover different topics such as the implementation of instruments of different nature for the OT estimate, the quantification of their reliability and the development of new light instrumentation. In this work, we present an automated system designed for continuous seeing measurements during day and night using multiple sensors. The system includes a fully automatic on-site platform that monitors operational status and delivers real-time information on sensor health and measurements. Its real-time acquisition capabilities enable the generation of local datasets, and allow on-site testing for forecasting methodologies.

Items.Authors: Mengmeng Qian, Jiahao Zhou, Wenfei Liu, Yingfu Wang, Haoyang Zhang, Kai Yun, Xianke Song, Hongzhuan Hu, Jianping Wang, Jiaru Chu, Ping Zhang, Zhigang Liu, Zengxiang Zhou
Items.Title: Real-Time Simulation and Control Platform for the LAMOST High-Density Fiber Positioning System
Items.Abstract: This work introduces a novel simulation and control system designed for the next-generation fiber positioning system of the LAMOST telescope upgrade. Facing a drastic miniaturization and a potential scale-up to over 10,000 units, the system overcomes the challenges of precise multi-unit coordination and real-time collision avoidance. Based on an asynchronous, event-driven architecture, the proposed solution achieves high-efficiency parallel processing for large-scale graphical rendering and motion planning. It has been successfully validated in both simulation and actual integration testing of the hybrid focal plane, demonstrating robust performance for future ultra-high-density spectroscopic surveys.

Items.Authors: Ivan A. Look, Skyler Padamada
Items.Title: Recoating efforts for the Tri-Annual CFHT Primary Mirror
Items.Abstract: Alongside CFHT’s strides toward upgrading the Building Facility are efforts made toward maintaining the current facility capabilities. One notable event is the planned triannual observatory shutdown, where the main objective is to recoat the telescope’s primary mirror. This paper provides a comprehensive breakdown of events that occurred during CFHT’s 2025 observatory shutdown.  The shutdown consists of four main stages: telescope disassembly, primary mirror cleaning/recoating, mirror cell support system inspection, and telescope reassembly. This process occurs over the course of about two weeks and requires help from a variety of disciplines, mainly (Operations, Instrumentation, and Software). The telescope disassembly effort may also include disconnecting the telescope’s Cassegrain environment for detailed inspection.   The Primary Mirror cleaning is a process that has evolved over many years and includes an intensive Mirror “wash and strip” procedure followed by the “re-al

Items.Authors: Neeraj K. Tiwari, Santosh V. Vadawale, Cherukari Sree Vaishnava, Mithun Neelkandan P. S., Hiteshkumar Lavjibhai Adalja
Items.Title: Reconfigurable Fizeau interferometry for surface-figure metrology of Wolter-I X-ray mirrors
Items.Abstract: At the Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), Ahmedabad, we are developing a Fizeau-interferometer–based metrology system for surface-figure measurement of Wolter-I X-ray mirrors. These paraboloid–hyperboloid mirrors are nearly conical, with micron-level deviation from the best-fit cone and typical half-cone angles of 0.5°–3°, requiring conical reference wavefronts for accurate testing. A Fizeau interferometer using a computer-generated hologram (CGH) can generate such wavefronts, but conventional approaches require multiple CGHs to test the various shells of nested X-ray telescopes. We present a conceptual interferometer design that enables measurement of mirrors across a range of half-cone angles using a single CGH. The approach modifies the output wavefront by adjusting the relative angle between the CGH and an additional optical element, allowing generation of the required conical wavefronts without changing the hologram. Analytical modelling and Zemax simulations are used to assess w

Items.Authors: Kevin Phan, J. Zachary Gazak
Items.Title: Relative-Brightness-Aware Quad Matching for Sparse-Field Astrometry
Items.Abstract: Narrow-field telescopes often detect too few stars for reliable catalog matching, making astrometric plate solving ambiguous. We introduce a magnitude-based enhancement to quad matching that incorporates relative brightness constraints derived from catalog inter-star magnitude differences (e.g., STTRC-7). Observed flux ratios are evaluated under a Bayesian decision process, where a lightweight reward–penalty function adjusts the Bayes factor for each quad based on agreement with expected brightness ordering. This down-weights geometrically plausible but photometrically inconsistent matches, improving convergence when only a small number of stars are visible. Across multiple sensors and sky regions, the method boosts solve rates by 15–30% in sparse fields and enables solutions with as few as five stars. The approach incurs negligible computational overhead and integrates seamlessly into existing plate-solving pipelines.

Items.Authors: David R. Andersen, Gelys Trancho, John Miles, Ryuji Suzuki, Ashley Baker, Kanaka Warad
Items.Title: Requirements management, performance budgeting, and traceability for the TMT first-light instruments
Items.Abstract: The TMT first-light instruments, IRIS, WFOS, and MODHIS, face demanding science goals and close integration with the observatory architecture including NFIRAOS, the facility AO system. We present the requirements management and performance budgeting framework developed to ensure scientific, functional, and interface compliance for the instruments. The approach includes requirement decomposition, flowdown, verification planning, and traceability within a configuration-controlled environment. We describe performance budgets for image quality, wavefront error, astrometry, and throughput, along with cross-instrument dependencies that require consistent modeling and disciplined change control. Examples illustrate reconciliation of science allocations with engineering estimates, resolution of interface issues, and the use of traceability tools. Finally, we recommend practices for multi-partner projects to reduce integration risk and support confidence in first-light performance.

Items.Authors: Xiaoyan Li, Xuefei Gong, Tingting Liu, Guang Yang, Zhengyang Li, Haikun Wen, Xiangyan Yuan
Items.Title: Research on key technologies of near-infrared survey telescope in Antarctica
Items.Abstract: Infrared astronomy is crucial for exploring the universe. Kunlun Station in Antarctica plateau has natural conditions such as dryness, coldness, and long polar nights, providing a unique advantage for near-infrared astronomical observations. However, it also faces challenges such as harsh environment, unattended operation, low power consumption requirements, and the easy formation of ice and frost on the mirror surface. This paper summarizes the advantages and challenges, the current situation and future planning of domestic and international infrared astronomy in Antarctica. The key technologies of Antarctica infrared telescopes also are analyzed, mainly including the performance of infrared detectors, suppression of instrument thermal self-emission, mirror surface de-icing and defrosting, optimization design of Dewars/cryostats, and cold optical systems, It could be referred to the future development of infrared telescopes in Antarctica.

Items.Authors: Pengfei Qiang, Lizhi Sheng, Yangji Yang
Items.Title: Research on key technology of soft X-ray focusing optical reflective coatings
Items.Abstract: Based on the eXTP satellite requirements, a Wolter-I focusing system was simulated with a 5250 mm focal length, 237 mm radius, 600 mm mirror length, and 45 layers. To optimize mirror coatings, the study examined surface roughness, mirror spacing, and materials using Monte Carlo simulations. Results show that dual-layer coatings, specifically Au+Ni4 and Au+C10, significantly enhance performance. With a mirror figure PV of 0.5 μm and RMS of 0.1 μm, the design achieved effective areas of 1000 cm² at 2 keV and 890 cm² at 6 keV. Furthermore, optimizing mirror spacing to 0.2 mm maximized the effective area while limiting stray light to below 4.8%.

Items.Authors: Jean-Michel Le Duigou, Denis Bausch, Nicolas Bray, Charles-Antoine Chevrier, Mathieu Clavery, Aurélie Courtois, Florent Gant, Brice Gorin, Pierre-Alain Goulm, Christophe Latry, Gauthier Malbrancke, Fredri Mirc, Alain Peus, Dorian Peyret, Bruno Regnier, Hélie Reininger, Mehdi Sodki
Items.Title: Results of the DICOS ground tests
Items.Abstract: DICOS is a technological demonstrator under a stratospheric balloon for advanced pointing and wavefront stability technologies. The current funded phase of the project ended in december 2025 with a full scale ground demonstration of the telescope mounted on a testing stand. Combining measurements on an artificial star and on sky observations of Polaris, we demonstrate a rejection of 500 of the gondola residual wobbling, estimated to 10-20 arcsec at 0.5 Hz. The limiting factors are the structural first modes at 12 and 22 Hz and the 3 ms time delay in the fast pointing loop. The slow AO loop reaches 5 mn WFE with a stability better than 1 nm over 10 hours, on the optical bench only. Unfortunately, the 40 cm aluminum main mirror has important high spatial frequencies that prevent the phase diversity to perform well at instrument level.

Items.Authors: José J. San Juan, Rosario Cosentino, Luca Di Fabrizio, Marcos Hernández Díaz, Héctor Ventura Pérez
Items.Title: Revamping the Visible low resolution spectrograph of the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo. Integrating legacy hardware into a modern web service architecture.
Items.Abstract: The continuous operation of astronomical instrumentation, such as LRS at the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo (TNG), frequently faces the challenge of "asymmetric obsolescence": while optical components and CCD sensors retain their scientific validity, the associated control interfaces and computing environments become outdated. This work details the reverse engineering and software development required to migrate the detector control system to a modern computing infrastructure.

Items.Authors: Hossein Mahmoodzadeh, Paolo Saracco, Ivan Di Antonio, Paolo Conconi, Diego Scaccabarozzi, Bortolino Saggin, Marco Riva, Emilio Molinari, Carmelo Arcidiacono, Ilaria Arosio, Enrico Cascone, Vincenzo Cianniello, Vincenz De Caprio, Gianluca Di Rico, Benedetta Di Francesco, Christian Eredia, Paolo Franzetti, Marco Fumana, Elisa Portaluri
Items.Title: Review of the optomechanical design of SHARP: a near infrared spectrograph for the next generation telescope
Items.Abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive overview of the last status of conceptual optomechanical design of SHARP, which has already been published as referenced paper in the Journal of Astronomical Telescopes, Instruments, and Systems (JATIS), including the optical architecture, mechanical structure, and key mechanisms developed to meet the demanding constraints imposed by the ELT environment. The optical design has been optimized to achieve high throughput and spectral performance while ensuring compactness and manufacturability under cryogenic and vacuum conditions.

Items.Authors: Tonya L. Peshel, Abigail Y. Pan, Tanmoy Chattopadhyay, Steven W. Allen, Marshall W. Bautz, Michael Cooper, Kevan Donlon, Catherine E. Grant, Sven Herrmann, Jill Juneau, Beverly J. LaMarr, Christopher Leitz, Adam B. Mantz, Eric D. Miller, R. Glenn Morris, Declan O'Neill, Peter Orel, Artem Poliszczuk, Gregory Prigozhin, Haley R. Stueber, Keith Warner
Items.Title: RNDR noise modeling in first-generation SiSeRO (Single-electron Sensitive Readout) devices
Items.Abstract: Flagship observatories require single-photon detectors with ultra-fast readout, sub-electron noise performance, and scalable large-format architectures. The X-ray Astronomy and Observational Cosmology group at Stanford, in collaboration with the MIT Kavli Institute and MIT Lincoln Laboratory, is developing readout technologies for next-generation charge-coupled devices (CCDs). Prototypes employing Single-electron Sensitive Readout (SiSeRO) amplifiers demonstrate excellent read noise and spectral performance using Repetitive Non-Destructive Readout (RNDR), achieving 0.5e- noise after just 57 cycles. However, a divergence from the expected trend with longer cycling suggests additional noise sources. In this paper, we present modeling predictions for probabilistic noise sources compared with new experimental results. Maturation of SiSeRO technology will improve detector performance at soft X-ray energies, and addressing technology gaps for future X-ray, UV/optical and NIR observatories.

Items.Authors: Sergey Naroenkov, Evgeniy A. Kopylov, Michael Nalivkin, Mansur Ibragimov, Mikhail Sachkov, Sergey Potanin, Lidiya Bolbasova
Items.Title: Russian-Cuban observatory: instruments and astroclimate
Items.Abstract: It is reported that the first telescope of the Russian-Cuban Observatory, installed at the observatory's optical station in Havana, Republic of Cuba, has begun operation. The tasks for observations that are supposed to be carried out using the mentioned telescope are described. The Russian-Cuban integration scheme is described and some of its features are briefly discussed. It is reported that the astroclimate has been measured at selected sites in Cuba, where the next stage of the observatory's construction is expected to be implemented.

Items.Authors: Andrea Di Paola, Roberto Speziali, Maurizio Oliviero, Luciano Dal Sasso, Vincenzo Mauriello, Mauro Centrone
Items.Title: SAMM 2.0: the upgraded Solar Activity Magnetic Monitor instrument for the SAMMNET Space Weather network
Items.Abstract: In June 2022, the first SAMM (Solar Activity Magnetic Monitor) prototype was installed at the INAF–Montemario Observatory in Rome, Italy, to test its space-weather monitoring capabilities. SAMM measures line-of-sight magnetic fields and Doppler velocities in the solar atmosphere at high cadence and at two heights, set by the MOF filters using potassium and sodium, probing the photosphere (~300 km) and chromosphere (~600 km). This dual-height sampling enables the first 3D reconstruction of these fields for improved forecasting. A new, upgraded version of SAMM has since been developed to provide stable, calibrated data for space-weather models. Its real-time magnetic-field and velocity maps make it uniquely suited to identify precursors of solar CMEs and flares. We present the new instrument, first-light images, performance estimates, and discuss its planned use in the SAMMNET network, an already funded network of three coordinated nodes.

Items.Authors: Clémentine Béchet, Michel Tallon, Isabelle Tallon-Bosc, Éric Thiébaut, Isaac Dinis, Caroline Kulcsár, Henri-François Raynaud, Nicolas Galland, Markus Kasper, Florian Ferreira, Maud Langlois, Emiliano Diolaiti, Anthony Boccaletti
Items.Title: SAXO+, the second-stage adaptive optics for SPHERE: continuous learning of the temporal dynamics of the wavefront
Items.Abstract: SAXO+ is designed to reduce the temporal error of the AO correction compared to the existing AO in SPHERE today, by including a second stage of AO working at a higher frequency (up to 2.7kHz) and by controlling it with algorithms using predictive features. Among those, we present here an algorithm with the particular asset that its control components are continuously learned and updated at every loop. An affine direct temporal model of the incoming aberrations is learned during closed-loop AO observations. A generalization of the Recursive Least Squares algorithm is used to update on the fly this predictive model, without the need to invert any large matrix. This predictive model is combined with an iterative controller designed to account at every loop for possible spatial and temporal variations of the data precision. We show that the continuous learning of the temporal model improves the predictive AO correction when vibrations are modelized in SAXO+ numerical simulations.

Items.Authors: Paul Fontanillas, Florian Ferreira, Arnaud Sevin, Damien Gratatdour, Chauvin Gaël, Emiliano Diolaiti, Raffaele Gratton, Magali Loupias, Julien Milli, François Wildi, Anthony Boccaletti
Items.Title: SAXO+, the second-stage adaptive optics for SPHERE: RTC final design and preliminary performance results
Items.Abstract: SAXO+ is the upgrade of the SPHERE adaptive optics (AO) system. After passing its Final Design Review  in April 2025 it entered the Assembly, Integration and Testing (AIT) phase in April 2026, with first light  scheduled for 2028 on the VLT. This upgrade aims to enhance the SPHERE’s contrast performance. This  second stage will feature a pyramid wavefront sensor (PWFS) operating at high frame rates up to 3 kHz and  a new deformable mirror (DM) with 952 actuators. In addition, SAXO+ will interface with the first stage  real-time controller (RTC), SPARTA. The SAXO+ RTC is based on the COSMIC platform for the hard real-  time layer and on the ESO RTC Toolkit for the soft real-time layer. Its modular design supports multiple  control strategies, including artificial intelligence (AI) approaches. This paper presents the RTC architecture,  the hardware interfaces integration and preliminary performance results from simulation and on bench.

Items.Authors: Isaac Bernardino Dinis, Nicolas Galland, Henri-François Raynaud, Caroline Kulcsár, Clémentine Béchet, Michel Tallon, Isabelle Tallon-Bosc, Maud Langlois, Florian Ferreira, François Wildi, Damien Ségransan, Anthony Boccaletti, Markus Kasper
Items.Title: SAXO+, the second-stage adaptive optics for SPHERE: single vs cascade control loop performance assessment
Items.Abstract: VLT-SPHERE is an adaptive optics and coronagraphic instrument at the VLT. SAXO+ aims to improve its performance by adding a second AO loop with a faster deformable mirror (2.7 kHz) and a more sensitive Pyramid WFS, cascaded with the current 41×41 HODM and Shack–Hartmann WFS running at 1.3 kHz. Although conceptually simple, this cascade adds control complexity, since two AO stages require jointly optimized controllers with challenging robustness and stability analyses.  This study assesses a hypothetical single-loop XAO architecture for SAXO+, where one controller drives both DMs. We show that it can match or, depending on the science case, improve performance relative to the cascade approach while simplifying control. The evaluation covers an Optimized Modal Gain Integrator and advanced controllers such as DD4AO and LQG.

Items.Authors: Mario Castro, Alvaro Quintana, Jorge Parra
Items.Title: SCADA system development for multiple telescopes employing a distributed and standardized architecture
Items.Abstract: .With the objective of increasing operational efficiency, the National Optical-Infrared Astronomy Research Laboratory (NOIRLab) is implementing tools that aim to optimize resource usage, downtime, maintenance strategies and gather useful data for smart decision-making. In this context NOIRLab will deploy a Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) for monitoring and controlling support systems for its main seven telescopes, including Vera C.Rubin. These systems will require data logging, plot historical and real time data, generate reports and alarm management.  NOIRLab’s approach is presented in order to create a reusable SCADA application across seven sites, including common software layer definitions, taxonomy-based tag tree construction and the use of standards and best practices for symbology, alarm configuration, and human machine interfaces. It is also shown the recommended server architecture that guarantees robustness, backup availability and interoperability across site

Items.Authors: Hans-Joachim Hess, Sriparsann S. Annadevara, Helmut Kravcar, Sebastian Steuer, Naman Pujari, Ralf Bender
Items.Title: Scaling PLC control systems for the MICADO cryostat: implementation and challenges
Items.Abstract: MICADO, the first-light instrument for the ESO Extremely Large Telescope (ELT), is currently in the integration and test phase of the project, with expected first light in 2030.  In large instrumentation projects the demand on sensors and actuators is often creating space issues for the control electronics. Considering this with respect to the MICADO cryostat, as well as its demanding cryogenic, operational, and integration requirements, we created a dedicated cryostat control system. A solution will be described for specific heater PCBs in conjunction with the traditional Beckhoff PLC system to ensure electromagnetic robustness for sensitive channel under all operational environmental conditions.  The selection process for off the-the-shelve PLC systems, the choice of terminals and the integration into a single instrument control system (ICS) is described in more detail for the ICS01 cryogenic-vacuum control cabinet, explaining the maintenance friendly cabling and repair concept.

Items.Authors: Fabrice Pancher, Sebastien Soler, Fabien Malbet, Hugo Rousset, Manon Lizzana, Alain Leger, Thierry Lepine, Florence Ardellier-Desages, Jerôme Amiaux, Pierre-Olivier Lagage
Items.Title: Setup and performance of focal-plane characterization benches for high-precision astrometry
Items.Abstract: Detecting Earth-like exoplanets requires micro-arcsecond astrometry, which relies on a precisely calibrated focal plane equipped with high-resolution detectors. Accurate calibration depends on characterizing detector imperfections and systematic effects. Optical benches have been developed to assess the sensor’s behavior: an integrating-sphere setup for electro-optical parameters, an interferometric bench for pixel-level geometry, and a star-field projection system for intrinsic distortion. This work presents the characterization benches built for a 46-MP imaging sensor, based on the same technology as the four 220-MP detectors foreseen for the final focal-plane, and the performance metrics obtained from these setups in the context of NASA’s HWO and ESA’s M-class missions. Upgrades will bring the test environment closer to operational conditions: a second 46-MP sensor will be added for multi-detector tests, plus an adjustable-angle fringe-projection system and improved alignment.

Items.Authors: Tristen M. Sextro, Randall L. McEntaffer, Nicolas M. Barrière, Ramses Günther, David Girou
Items.Title: Silicon pore optics spectrograph architecture for future explorer-class soft X-ray missions
Items.Abstract: Future soft X-ray astronomy missions require compact, lightweight spectrographs capable of high spectral resolution within mass and volume limits of explorer-class spacecraft. Silicon Pore Optics (SPO) developed by cosine and ESA have emerged as a leading technology for X-ray telescopes for their low mass, high stiffness, and modular fabrication. This work investigates an SPO-based spectrograph concept where primary focusing optics and diffraction elements are made using SPO manufacturing techniques. By engineer-matching focal length, pore geometry, and alignment tolerances between mirror and grating, a system can be optimized as a unified instrument rather than a combination of independent components. The design is evaluated with ray-tracing simulations to assess resolving power, throughput, and sensitivity to alignment errors. This approach aims to pioneer the SPO mirror + SPO reflection grating architecture as a path toward future spectroscopy-dedicated missions in X-ray astronomy.

Items.Authors: Pascal Jaufmann, Jörg-Uwe Pott, Oliver Sawodny
Items.Title: Simulation of LGS-based vibration mitigation for large telescopes
Items.Abstract: Diffraction-limited imaging in large telescopes requires mitigation of both atmospheric and structural disturbances in the optical system. Therefore, all disturbance acting on the adaptive optics (AO) system must be estimated and compensated for in real-time. We present and compare different methods for the estimation and control of high-frequency vibrations using already available wavefront data from laser guide stars. This includes an integrator combined with a Kalman filter as well as linear quadratic Gaussian control. The designs are validated within a realistic end-to-end AO simulation fed by telemetry data from the Very Large Telescope.

Items.Authors: Alexis Lau, A. J. Eldorado Riggs, Susan Redmond, Eric J. Cady, John E. Krist, Iva Laginja, Dan Sirbu, Sophie Noiret, Alexis Bidot
Items.Title: Simulation tools for realistic high-order wavefront correction with the Roman Coronagraph
Items.Abstract: NASA's Roman Space Telescope carries the Coronagraph Instrument to perform the first high-contrast imaging of exoplanets in space. The instrument’s only top-level requirement is to demonstrate a broadband dark zone. The Community Participation Program (CPP) is planning a range of scientific and engineering activities to perform afterward. To provide realistic simulations of Roman Coronagraph performance in these various modes, the CPP’s Hardware Working Group is developing the corgihowfsc software package. This repository is a wrapper combining several other repositories open-sourced by the Roman Coronagraph project and CPP: corgisim for producing realistic images, cgi-howfsc for performing and high-order wavefront sensing and control (HOWFSC), cgi-eetc for exposure time calculation, and cgi-coralign for performing optical calibrations. By using this collection of official modeling tools, the modeling results from the CPP will be the highest possible fidelity.

Items.Authors: Luca Cortese, Carmelo Arcidiacono, Giuseppe Viterbo, Matteo Simioni, Fabio Rossi, Alessio Turchi, Alfio T. Puglisi, Guido Agapito, Daniele Vassallo, Lorenzo Merli, Elena Masciadri, Enrico Pinna, Francesco Maio, Davide Fedele, Arseniy Kuznetsov
Items.Title: Simulation-based Inference of atmospheric parameters from adaptive optics telemetry data
Items.Abstract: Inferring atmospheric parameters for observational astronomy is important for different reasons, such as the evaluation and characterization of astronomical sites and point spread function estimation.  This could be performed by exploiting telemetry data saved by Adaptive Optics (AO) systems. Particularly, the estimation of parameters such as horizontal wind speed, wind direction and turbulence profiles using those data is a challenging task, given also the presence of intrinsic degeneracies.  In order to face this problem, we aim to perform amortized Bayesian posterior estimation with a Simulation-Based Inference approach (SBI). This method makes use of Neural Networks (NNs) as density estimators acting in the (parameters, data) space. The dataset used to train the model is generated with the end-to-end AO simulator SPECULA.   This method provides sub-second inference and could be adapted to real data via fine-tuning.

Items.Authors: Mary Kreidel, Byeongho Eom, Henry LeDuc, Peter Day
Items.Title: Simulations of aluminum resonant absorbers for energy-resolving mid-IR MKIDs
Items.Abstract: Mid-infrared detectors with high sensitivity and stability are essential for spectroscopic and interferometric studies of exoplanets orbiting nearby stars. Spectroscopic detectors can monitor star-exoplanet systems for transit and phase curve variations, and in interferometric applications, starlight is suppressed to enable individual photon detection. Kinetic inductance detector (KID) arrays developed for the far-infrared (240–25 µm) have recently set new benchmarks in both performance aspects, utilizing a resonant absorber design that allows otherwise highly-reflective aluminum to become about 75% absorptive at the targeted frequency[1]. Here, we discuss the design of KID arrays for the mid-infrared band (20–4 µm). We describe simulations of resonant absorbers for that wavelength that take into account high frequency effects, such as reduced skin depth. We predict the performance of our designs in the mid-infrared by scaling our results at 25 µm.  [1] Phys. Rev. X 14, 041005 (2024)

Items.Authors: Matteo Di Carlo, Mauro Dolci, Ugur Ylmaz
Items.Title: ska-tango-exporter: a diagnostic tool for analyzing interrelated problems in the TANGO-controls environment, tailored to the needs of the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) project.
Items.Abstract: The ska-tango-exporter is a diagnostic tool designed to extract comprehensive information from a TANGO-controls–based system deployed in a Kubernetes cluster (within a continuous integration/continuous deployment – CI/CD context). Its purpose is to support the analysis of complex, interconnected problems that are often difficult to manage with standard tools.  It leverages existing data sources such as the TANGO database and Kubernetes’ etcd, together with internal monitoring systems including Prometheus (for attribute collection in a polling fashion) and InfluxDB (for event tracking). Starting from TANGO v10, the exporter can also enable OpenTelemetry metrics, providing a standardized way to integrate with modern observability platforms and extend monitoring capabilities.

Items.Authors: Ravinder K. Banyal, Gurwinder Singh, Ayan Sahoo, Arun Surya
Items.Title: SLODAR-based atmospheric turbulence profiler
Items.Abstract: Accurate characterization of atmospheric turbulence, described by the Fried parameter r₀, is essential for optimizing adaptive optics (AO) on large telescopes. AO improves ground-based observations by correcting turbulence-induced wavefront errors. We present the design and development of a Slope Detection and Ranging (SLODAR) instrument to measure how seeing varies with altitude. Using the open-source HCiPy package, we simulate phase screens, wavefront propagation, and Shack–Hartmann spot patterns at different heights. The instrument will provide direct, altitude-resolved turbulence profiles that complement simulations and allow cross-validation under real conditions. By comparing profiles from both methods, we assess the accuracy of SLODAR in reconstructing atmospheric structure. This combined approach improves understanding of turbulence dynamics and supports the development and implementation of advanced adaptive optics system for India's proposed National Large Optical Telescope.

Items.Authors: Willem J. van der Westhuizen, Eben P. Wiid, Lisa A. Crause, Danièl Groenewald, Encarni Romero Colmenero, Nico van der Merwe, Francois Strumpfer, Michael Sam, Tasheen Naicker, Chrey M. Sookha, Sam Ndumo, Etienne L. Simon, Thabelo Makananise, Johan Hendricks, Denville Gibbons, Nicolaas Jacobs, Shamiel Adams, Sunnyboy Kabini, Devakshan Naicker, Anthony Koeslag, Willa de Water, Jonathan Pieterse, Lizette Labuschagne, John A. Booth, Hermanus J. Kriel, John W. Menzies, Lee Townsend, Rudi Kuhn
Items.Title: Southern African Large Telescope (SALT) shutdown 2025
Items.Abstract: SALT performs its major maintenance activities, to maintain the observatory's performance and reliability, during shutdown periods scheduled roughly every two years. The telescope is taken offline entirely, meaning all scientific observations cease, affording the mechanical, electronic, and software teams full access to the telescope to conduct intensive work that is impossible during normal operations.  The 2025 shutdown was from 24 March to 13 May and this period was dedicated to an unprecedented global tilt of the primary mirror array, adjusting the 91 segments to correct positional discrepancies that had developed over time. Comprehensive maintenance, repairs and upgrades were also done across various telescope systems, including the replacement of aging components, such as seals or degraded sensors to prevent future failures. These intervals also allow us to inspect and clean all optics, which degrade due to environmental factors such as dust or contamination from insects and bats.

Items.Authors: Federico Battaini, Kalyan Radhakrishnan, Simone Di Filippo, Pietro Schipani, Riccardo Claudi, Mirko Colapietro
Items.Title: SOXS at NTT: results and lesson learned during the preliminary acceptance in Europe phase
Items.Abstract: The Son Of X-Shooter (SOXS) is the specialized spectroscopy-follow-up facility for transient event with a flexible scheduler at the ESO NTT. The instrument spans from 350nm up to 2000nm with an average of R∼4500 for a 1” slit. Currently, SOXS is installed at the telescope in the scientific commissioning phase. In December 2024 we completed the Preliminary Acceptance in Europe (PAE) of the instrument after the ESO revision. We report here on the performances assessed in that phase, the lesson learned for future instruments, the corrective activities and the tools prepared for the AIV/commissioning at the telescope.

Items.Authors: Varun Kabra, SPT-3G+ Collaboration
Items.Title: SPT-3G+ readout design and characterization
Items.Abstract: SPT-3G+ is a new camera for the South Pole Telescope (SPT) designed to measure the cosmic microwave background (CMB). It consists of 24,000 superconducting transition-edge sensor (TES) bolometers in 90/150GHz polarization-sensitive dichroic pixels that operate at 100mK. The cryogenic readout wiring consists of 28 microwave frequency (4-8 GHz) channels (RF) and direct current bias lines (DC) that are arranged into readout harnesses from 300K-4K, before branching off to individual detector module assemblies from 4K-100mK. The detector module also includes magnetic shielding, which has been modeled to provide sufficient shielding for the detectors and readout components. We will present a summary of the SPT-3G+ readout design, including simulations of the thermal and magnetic shielding performance, and describe initial characterization of readout components and the entire chain.

Items.Authors: Melissa Flores, Alexa LaPinta, John D. Monnier, James Cutler, Leonid Pogorelyuk
Items.Title: STARI fiber-injection prototype testing and simulation
Items.Abstract: The STarlight Acquisition and Reflection toward Interferometry (STARI) is a NASA-funded joint mission to advance technology for future space interferometry with two 8U cubeSATs to collect/transfer starlight between each other using a single mode fiber. We present a lab proof-of-concept for a two satellite system demonstrating fiber-coupling and simulations for starlight transmission between satellites.The first payload is the Pupil Transport (PT) that collects the incoming starlight and reflects it into the other spacecraft. The second is the Fiber Injection and Detection (FID) that injects the reflected starlight into a single-mode fiber on the other spacecraft and uses itself as a reference. In the lab set-up, we achieve a 20% match to the simulation results for optimal coupling efficiency. This level of coupling efficiency can then be used in future missions to collect meteorology data on stars and exoplanets using formation flying fiber coupled systems.

Items.Authors: Lorenzo Merli, Daniele Vassallo, Elena Carolo, Simone Di Filippo, Tânia Gomes Machado, Paolo Cerpelloni, Alessandro Lorenzetto, Domenico Barbato, Dino Mesa, Cecilia Lazzoni, Luca Marafatto, Jacopo Farinato, Maria Bergomi, Fulvio Laudisio, Davide Ricci, Gabriele Umbriaco
Items.Title: Statistical analysis and future improvement of SHARK-NIR calibration and post-processing pipeline
Items.Abstract: SHARK-NIR is a near-infrared coronagraph installed at LBT. By leveraging the LBT adaptive optics systems, the instrument is optimized to perform high contrast imaging using a variety of coronagraphic techniques.  SHARK-NIR is currently in its early science phase, during which it has already executed several observing runs and accumulated many hours of scientific exposures and technical calibration data.  We used those data to conduct a set of statistical analyses aimed at validating the calibration pipelines and assessing the overall behavior of the instrument. In this contribution, we present the results of these studies, with particular emphasis on the management of non-common path aberrations (NCPA), the characterization of residual jitter, and the evaluation of the accuracy of the technical exposure time calculator. We further discuss how these results drive potential improvements to the calibration procedures, the instrument’s operational strategies and post-processing techniques.

Items.Authors: Silvia Micheli, Alessia Ritacco, Jonathan Aumont, Stefano Berta, Ludovico Bizzarri, François Boulanger, Alessandro Carones, Andrea Catalano, Francesco Cuttaia, Anne Denis, Francois-Xavier Désert, Anne-Laure Fontana, David González Ovejero, Benedetta Kalemi, Nicoletta Krachmalnicoff, Samuel Leclercq, Juan Francisco Macias-Pérez, Bruno Maffei, Marina Migliaccio, Ludovic Montier, Pascal Morfin, Michel Moulin, Louise Mousset, Matteo Murgia, Federico Nati, Pierluigi Ortu, Michel Pérault, Giampaolo Pisano, Tonino Pisanu, Nicolas Ponthieu, Sofia Savorgnano, Luca Terenzi, Louis Thibaut, Jeanne Treuttel, Christophe Vescovi, Léo Vacher, Mario Zannoni
Items.Title: Status and future development of the COSMOCal Project for absolute CMB polarization calibration
Items.Abstract: CMB polarization measurements are pushing instrumental sensitivities to levels where calibration systematics become a dominant limitation. The large dynamic range between cosmological and Galactic emission prevents future experiments from relying only on diffuse sky measurements or standard celestial calibrators. To address this challenge, we propose an artificial calibration source deployed as a guest payload on a geostationary satellite, scheduled for launch by the Eutelsat group by 2030. This source will provide stable, well-characterized polarized microwave signals accessible to multiple ground-based observatories. In 2024, a first demonstrator of this concept was assembled and tested at the IRAM 30m telescope (Ritacco+24 PASP), validating key aspects of the design and observing strategy. I will present the project status, the updated development timeline, and the refined scientific and technical requirements, defined with the observatories that plan to use this calibration source.

Items.Authors: Medha Chakraborty, On behalf of NectarCAM consortium and CTAO consortium
Items.Title: Status of the NectarCAM Camera for the Medium-Sized Telescopes of CTAO
Items.Abstract: NectarCAM is a camera designed to detect Cherenkov light from gamma rays in the energy range from roughly 100 GeV to 30 TeV and will equip medium-sized telescopes (MSTs) of the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO). The camera consists of 1855 pixels, each comprising a photomultiplier tube with an associated light guide. The Front-End electronics is based on the NECTAr chip, which integrates a 1 GHz switched-capacitor array sampler and a 12-bit ADC. The first camera has been extensively tested and is scheduled for shipment in 2026, while testing and integration work are ongoing for subsequent cameras. During the validation process, the NectarCAM units undergo a wide range of performance tests, including studies of their thermal behavior, thanks to the thermally controlled darkroom at CEA Paris-Saclay, which can reach temperatures as low as -15 °C. Details of the integration status, ongoing upgrades, and the test results will be presented at the conference.

Items.Authors: Lucijana Stanic, Ivan Cardea, Edoardo Charbon, Domenico Della Volpe, Daniel Florin, Andrea Guerrieri, Gilles Koziol, Etienne Lyard, Nicolas Produit, Aramis Raiola, Prasenjit Saha, Vitalii Sliusar, Achim Vollhardt, Roland Walter
Items.Title: Stellar kinematics from a time-asymmetric Hanbury Brown–Twiss Effect
Items.Abstract: Intensity interferometry has recently reemerged as a powerful method for high-angular resolution astronomy. In this work, we demonstrate that it can also be used to probe internal stellar kinematics through a time-asymmetric Hanbury Brown and Twiss (HBT) effect.  We develop a numerical framework that incorporates Doppler-induced phase terms into a spatio-temporal visibility function and simulated this effect for two astrophysical cases: an emission-line Be-star disk and an absorption-line spectroscopic binary.  Our results suggest that, with modern single-photon detectors providing picosecond time resolution and narrowband filtering, this effect could offer a new, complementary method for measuring stellar kinematics in the time domain.  In parallel, efforts toward a laboratory demonstration of the time-asymmetric HBT effect using controlled wavelength offsets as an analogue to Doppler shifts are being pursued.

Items.Authors: Max N. Brodheim, Eric Jeschke, Kyle Westfall, Debora Pelliccia, Xavier Prochaska, Joseph F. Hennawi, Ryan Cooke, Bradford Holden, John O'Meara, Jeffery Mader
Items.Title: Streamlining Spectroscopic Observations: A Real-Time Data Reduction Display for Keck and Beyond
Items.Abstract: In 2025, the W. M. Keck Observatory released a “Quick Look” real-time spectroscopic data reduction graphical user interface (GUI) for several of its instruments. Built upon the open-source PypeIt data reduction pipeline, the tool provides automated image and wavelength calibration, global and local sky subtraction, flexure compensation, and spectral extraction. Leveraging PypeIt’s configuration-driven architecture and standardized data models, the GUI requires no observatory-specific code once a spectrograph has been integrated into PypeIt’s library of over 50 supported instruments (including echelle, multi-object, and long-slit), offering a near turn-key solution for real-time data assessment. This paper summarizes the features of the tool, how to integrate a new spectrograph, and future features in development.

Items.Authors: Nolan McPhaul, Randall McEntaffer, Ningxiao Zhang, Fabien Grise, Jake McCoy
Items.Title: Stretchy gratings: fabricating a custom-groove-patterned grating by manipulating parallel-groove patterns
Items.Abstract: We present a novel fabrication method for a custom-groove-patterned diffraction grating inspired by  astronomical ultraviolet (UV) and X-ray applications. By manipulating the parallel-groove pattern  from an optical grating on a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) stamp, we produced a fanned-out groove  profile. We created a differential strain field across the 3000 nm period grating by applying two  different strains to the top and bottom, stretching perpendicular to the groove direction, resulting  in a period varying from 3057 nm to 3207 nm across the centimeter long grooves. By replicating the  paths of converging light within astronomical telescopes, this fanned-out groove pattern should lead to higher  resolution spectroscopy. Future prospects for this method are discussed in comparison to other modern  fabrication methods.

Items.Authors: Jonathan Steiner, Joel Payne, Jason N. Worden, John S. Hudek, Dennis McBride, Grant Hill, Matt Wahl, Ed Wetherell, Adan Rodrigues, Tod Von Boeckmann, Eric Levine, Obediah Levine, Shawn Guerpo, Shawn Tapang, Chris Funada, Danny Baldwin, Steven Baca, Derek Park, Dan Orr, James Chong, Chris Martins, Robert Harrington, Mark Devenot, Joseph Rounsaville, Justin Ballard, Jerez Tehero, Hamza Elwir, Michael Dayawon, Tyler Coda, Greg Doppmann, Keith Vachon, Leslie Wold, Jeremy Zambeck
Items.Title: Structural Pier Repair, Full-scale Implementation of Grout Replacement on Keck I Telescope.
Items.Abstract: Each of the Keck telescopes incorporates a 3” thick layer of grout which serves as the primary load path between the steel azimuth journal—the telescope’s running surface—and the main body of the reinforced concrete pier. Over the past ~20 years Keck has observed increased journal deflections of the Keck 1 telescope under load. These increased deflections affect telescope pointing and can cause azimuth drive faults.     This paper presents: 1) lessons learned and changes made between the trial repair and two major “production” downtimes (each 5-6 weeks) which occurred in 2025, including logistical improvements, new tooling, addressing learning curves with contracting teams, and process updates like dust control; all resulting in improved efficiency. 2) An update on oil seepage mitigation efforts – oil exposure being a likely root cause of the grout deterioration. 3) Results from the total three repairs done to date.

Items.Authors: Ashesh Abhisek Khatua, Jón Emil Guðmundsson, Xiaodong Ren, Thomas Gascard, Rustam Balafendiev
Items.Title: Studying the systematics of CMB telescopes using finite-difference-time-domain simulations
Items.Abstract: We present MeepSAT (MEEP Simulation and Analysis for Telescopes), an ongoing effort to develop a Finite-Difference-Time-Domain (FDTD) simulation framework (based on an open-source code called MEEP) for analysing the optical systematics of cosmic microwave background (CMB) telescopes. MeepSAT will allow us to shed light on some systematics caused by effects that current industry-standard physical optics and ray-tracing softwares have a hard time modeling. This includes near-field interactions of sub-wavelength structures embedded in larger optical systems, the impact of absorptive elements placed outside of the optical path, non-uniform material properties, and effects related to baffles. We benchmark the MeepSAT simulations against other softwares using a simple single-lens telescope and demonstrate its advanced capabilities using more complex refractive systems.
